meta.blurb: A hundred-year-old little book with one big idea: your thoughts are seeds, and your life is the garden that grows from them. James Allen shows how the mind shapes character, health, goals and peace.
meta.bible: James Allen: English writer (1864 to 1912) who published As a Man Thinketh in 1903; a short, quiet book, not a full treatise. As a Man Thinketh: the title comes from the Book of Proverbs (23:7), as a man thinks in his heart, so he is. Seven parts: Thought and Character; Effect of Thought on Circumstances; Effect of Thought on Health and the Body; Thought and Purpose; The Thought-Factor in Achievement; Visions and Ideals; Serenity. Key images: the mind as a Garden, thoughts as Seeds, Weeds, Corn and Nettles, the Mirror, the Anchor, the Jewel of Wisdom, the Rock in the storm. Allen's three short sayings: Self-control is strength, Right Thought is mastery, Calmness is power. Allen's ideas about thought and illness are an old opinion, not modern medicine. Voice and tone: calm, encouraging and plain, a quiet teacher speaking to one reader; retold in our own words and attributed to Allen.

B1B2: James Allen wrote As a Man Thinketh in 1903, and it is only a short book. He hoped that it would make readers stop and think about how their minds work.
Allen says that the mind is the master power that shapes a person's character and life. Whatever a man thinks about most, he slowly turns into.
Every person builds his own life with his thoughts, and he can also destroy it in the same way. Nobody else holds the tools, so nobody else can do the work for him.
The title comes from a line in the Book of Proverbs: as a man thinks in his heart, so he is. Allen builds his whole book on this one simple idea.
A person's character is not an accident, because it is made from all the thoughts he has had. Good habits of thought make a good character, and careless habits make a weak one.
Allen compares the mind to a garden that can be looked after with care or left to grow wild. Either way, something is going to grow there, because the soil is never empty.
If you plant no useful seeds, weeds will arrive by themselves and take over the soil. A wise gardener removes the weeds and plants flowers and fruit in their place.
By doing this work, we learn how thought really works and how our own minds grow. In time, a person becomes the careful gardener of his own soul.
Every action begins as a thought, even when the thought is so quick that we do not notice it. Joy and suffering are the fruit that grows from those thoughts.
Allen says that good thoughts can only bring good results, and bad thoughts can only bring bad ones. In the same way, nothing can grow from corn except corn, and nothing from nettles except nettles.
The law of cause and effect is fair, and no one stands outside us to punish or reward us. We simply meet the results of the thoughts we have chosen to keep.
A person who wants to be better must begin by changing what he thinks about. Change does not happen by wishing, because it needs effort every day.
Allen says that even a weak person can grow strong, but only by his own steady effort. Nobody can carry him to strength, and no one can take his place in the work.
In the second part of the book, Allen turns from the mind to the world around us. He asks how our thoughts are connected to the things that happen in our lives.
He says that our outer life is like a mirror, which shows what is going on inside us. The seeds of thought grow into the situations we live in.
Many people want better circumstances, but they are not willing to improve themselves. That is why, Allen says, they so often stay in the same place.
We cannot always choose what happens to us, but we can always choose what we think. By choosing our thoughts, we slowly shape the life we find ourselves in.
It is easy to blame other people, bad luck or the times we live in. Allen says this habit only keeps us weak, because it gives away our power.
A hard moment does not make a person what he is; it shows him what he already is. That is why trouble can teach us more than comfort.
Allen warns us not to judge others by what they own or by what they suffer. We cannot see the long struggle that lies behind a person's life.
Suffering can be a teacher, and it often points to a lesson we have not yet learned. When we finally understand it, the pain has done its work and can go.
A man who turns away from his harmful thoughts will soon notice changes in his daily life. As his mind becomes cleaner, better things seem to come toward him.
In Allen's view, we receive only what we have earned by our own thoughts and efforts. Luck matters much less than most people believe it does, he says.
The next part of the book is about the body, which Allen says is the servant of the mind. It follows the orders of the mind, whether they are given on purpose or not.
Allen believed that fear, anger and worry could make the body weak and ill. He thought a mind full of these feelings would slowly wear down the person.
Today, doctors know that illness has many causes, and thoughts are only one of them. So this part of the book is not medical advice, and a sick person should always see a doctor.
Calm and happy thoughts, on the other hand, seem to bring a light step and a kind face. Allen says that a cheerful mind is the best friend a person's body can have.
In the fourth part of the book, Allen talks about the need for a purpose in life. People without a clear goal often feel lost, and they fall into worry, fear and self-pity.
He asks the reader to choose one clear and honest goal and to set his heart on it. A goal that gives life a direction is better than a hundred scattered wishes.
Make your purpose the centre of your thoughts, and return to it every day. Allen says it will hold you steady like an anchor in a storm.
Doubt and fear are the great enemies of a goal, and Allen says they must be driven out. A man who lets them stay has already half failed.
You will make mistakes on the way, but each failure can teach you something useful. Allen says that a person who keeps learning is already moving toward success.
When thought and purpose join together, a person's power grows quickly. He stops drifting, takes his own place in the world and becomes able to do real work.
The fifth part of the book explains that all achievement, large or small, begins in thought. Before anyone builds a thing, he has already built it in his mind.
Allen says that a man who wants to achieve little needs to give up little. A man who wants to achieve a great deal must give up a great deal.
To rise higher, a person must let go of laziness, fear and selfish thoughts. These habits keep us low, and each one has to be replaced by something better.
Allen says that the same law works in business, in study and in the life of the spirit. In each of them, the reward belongs to the person who thinks clearly and works steadily.
Good results seldom arrive in a day, so patience is part of the work. Allen says that the person who keeps going calmly will be there when the harvest comes.
The sixth part of the book is about visions and ideals. Allen says that dreamers are the people who save the world.
Without its dreamers, the world would have no new roads, no great buildings and no new ideas. Allen says that every great builder, thinker and teacher began with a vision.
The picture you hold in your mind and the ideal you carry in your heart are what you will slowly become. So look after them as you would look after something precious.
Imagine a young worker in a small, dull job who dreams of a bigger life. Allen says that this inner picture will pull him forward until his outer life begins to match it.
Your dream will be tested, and there will be days when it seems very far away. Hold on to it with patience, because a dream that survives these days grows stronger.
The last part of the book is about serenity, which means a deep and quiet peace of mind. Allen calls this calm one of the most beautiful jewels of wisdom.
A calm person has spent a long time learning to rule his own thoughts. Because he understands how his own mind works, he also understands other people better.
An angry or anxious mind is like a stormy sea that throws everything about. A calm mind, however, is like a rock that the waves cannot move.
Near the end, Allen sums up the lesson in three short and simple ideas. He says that self-control is strength, that right thought is mastery, and that calmness is power.
When your thoughts become wild and restless, speak to them gently, as you would speak to a tired child. Tell them to be quiet and still, and then wait.
The message of the book is simple: you are the maker of your own character. Your mind is the gardener, and every thought is a seed.
Choose your thoughts carefully, because over time they will become your actions, your habits and your life. The book is more than a hundred years old, but its advice is still easy to try today.
C1C2: James Allen, an English writer who lived a quiet and thoughtful life, published As a Man Thinketh in 1903 as a very short book. He described it in his foreword as the fruit of long meditation and experience, offered not as a full treatise but as a suggestion. His hope was simply that every reader would be moved to look for the truth within his own mind.

At the heart of the book lies a bold claim: that the mind is the master power, moulding and making every part of a human life. Thought is the chisel, and character is the statue that slowly emerges from the waiting stone, one small cut at a time. Whatever a person has become, Allen argues, he became by thinking his way there.

Allen insists that every person is the maker of himself, shaping his own fortunes in the quiet workshop of the mind. The same tools that can build a noble life can also pull it down, and the choice of how to use them is never taken away. No one else can do this work on our behalf, for no one else lives inside our thoughts.

The title is borrowed from a line in the Book of Proverbs, which says that as a man thinks in his heart, so he is. Allen treats this ancient sentence as a plain statement of fact, a law that works as steadily as the pull of gravity. Everything else in the little book is, in effect, a commentary upon those few words.

A person's character, Allen explains, is no accident of birth or luck, but the complete sum of all his thoughts. Each habitual thought leaves a trace, much as a footpath is worn into the grass by many feet. In the same way, a generous mind and a bitter mind are both built, patiently and unseen, from small repeated acts of attention.

The writer likens the human mind to a garden, one that may be cultivated with intelligence or abandoned to run wild. Either way, the soil will not stay empty, because it is the nature of a garden to produce something. The only real choice is whether the crop will be one we planned or one that simply arrived.

If useful seeds are not sown, Allen observes, a rich crop of weeds will spring up uninvited and choke the ground. The wise gardener therefore uproots every false, impure and useless thought, and plants in its place the flowers and fruits of right thinking. By continuing in this way, a person sooner or later becomes the master gardener of his own soul.

Through such patient work, a person learns how thought acts upon the self, and he comes to understand the laws by which his own mind grows. The knowledge arrives slowly, in the way that a gardener learns about soil and season only by tending one particular plot. Gradually the garden becomes a patient teacher as well as a task to be done.

Every deed, Allen argues, is the blossom of an earlier thought, even when the thought passed so quickly that its owner never noticed it. Joy and suffering alike are the fruit of what has been planted in the mind. A man who studies this chain of cause and effect begins to see that his life is far less a matter of chance than he supposed.

Good thoughts and good deeds cannot possibly yield a bad harvest, nor can bitter thoughts and deeds yield a sweet one. As Allen puts it, nothing can come from corn except corn, and nothing from nettles except nettles. People readily understand this law in the natural world, yet strangely few of them apply it to the world of the mind.

The law that governs these things is perfectly just, and no outside power waits to reward or punish us. We are not sentenced by a judge, but simply meet the plain consequences of the thoughts that we have been willing to entertain. This is a stern teaching, though Allen finds in it a source of great hope, since a cause can always be changed.

Anyone who longs to be better must therefore begin where character begins, which is in the mind. Wishing alone has never altered anything, for improvement demands honest effort, repeated daily and often against the pull of old habit. The man who is willing to make that effort, Allen assures us, will find that the door to change was never locked.

Even the weakest of men, Allen claims, may grow strong, but he can do so only by his own labour and persistence. No one else can carry him into strength, and no one else can take his place at the work. Strength, like every worthwhile skill, is built up by exercise rather than handed over as a gift.

In the second part of the book, Allen turns from the inner life of thought to the outer world of circumstances. He wants to show that the two are far more closely bound together than most people suspect. What happens to us, he suggests, is not nearly so separate from what happens within us as it first appears.

Our outward life, he writes, is a kind of mirror in which the secret contents of the mind are reflected for all to see. The seeds of thought that we allow to take root in the heart eventually blossom into the situations we find ourselves living in. Whatever the soul quietly harbours will, in time, show its face in the world.

Many people are eager to improve their circumstances, yet remain unwilling to improve themselves, and so they stay exactly where they are. Allen regards this as the great mistake, since the outer conditions of a life are tied to the inner man by invisible cords. A person who refuses to change within cannot expect to be rewarded with change without.

A man cannot always choose the circumstances he is born into or meets, but he can choose the thoughts he thinks, and so, indirectly, shape his fate. Every thought is a small decision about the kind of person he will become. By these decisions he is slowly steering his life, whether he realises it or not.

It is tempting to blame other people, bad luck or the age we live in for the troubles that we face. Allen believes that this habit is a poison, because it hands our power over to forces we cannot control. Only when we accept that we are the cause of our own condition do we regain the ability to improve it.

A crisis, Allen observes, does not make a person what he is, but merely reveals to him what he already was. A man who thinks himself kind may discover, under pressure, a selfish temper he never suspected. For this reason, the hardest hours of life are often the most instructive, since they hold up an honest mirror.

Allen is careful to warn readers against judging others by what they own or by what they endure. Poverty is not always the punishment of a wicked heart, and wealth is not always the reward of a virtuous one. Only the person himself can know the long struggle that lies hidden behind his circumstances.

Suffering, he says, is a teacher that never goes away until the lesson has been learned. It points to some error of thought that we have not yet noticed, and it presses upon us until we finally pay attention. When the lesson is understood and the thinking has changed, the pain has accomplished its purpose and quietly departs.

When a man turns with resolve from his harmful and selfish thoughts, Allen says, the effect upon his daily life will soon be visible. As his mind grows cleaner, his habits, his relationships and his work begin to improve alongside it. The change may at first seem small, yet it carries within it the promise of a very different future.

In Allen's view, every person receives exactly what he has earned through his own thoughts and efforts, and not one grain more. Windfalls and strokes of luck may seem to contradict this, but he suggests that they matter far less than the slow harvest of a steady character. The sober lesson is that there are no shortcuts to a character worth having.

The third part of the book turns to the body, which Allen describes as the faithful servant of the mind. It obeys the orders that thought gives it, whether those orders are chosen deliberately or allowed to slip out unawares. The face, the posture and the very manner of a person's movements thus become a kind of handwriting of the mind.

Allen was convinced that fear, anger and anxiety could wear down the body as surely as hard labour or poor food. A mind crowded with these feelings, he thought, would sooner or later betray itself in the sufferer's health. He wrote at the beginning of the twentieth century, long before medicine had studied stress as it does today.

Modern doctors know that illness has many causes, among them heredity, infection, accident and age, and that thoughts are only one thread in this web. This section of Allen's book should therefore be read as an old opinion about mind and body, and it is not medical advice. Anyone who is unwell should consult a qualified doctor rather than rely on thought alone.

Calm, cheerful and generous thoughts, on the other hand, seem to lend the face a quiet beauty and the step a certain lightness. Allen believed that a contented mind is the best companion a body can have, and that a sour temper soon shows itself in the features. Whatever we make of this claim, few would deny that a person at peace is a pleasanter person to meet.

In the fourth part, Allen turns to purpose, without which, he says, a person drifts like a boat that has lost both rudder and oar. Those without a goal fall easily into worry, fear and self-pity, and these feelings are simply signs of a mind with nothing to steer by. Aimless thought, in other words, is a kind of weather that blows us wherever it likes.

He therefore asks the reader to choose one clear and honourable goal, and to set his heart upon it without reserve. A single purpose, held firmly, gives a life its direction in the same way that a compass needle guides a ship across the open sea. It is far better than a hundred scattered wishes, none of which is ever followed through to its end.

Make your purpose the centre of your thoughts, Allen advises, and return to it each morning as a traveller returns to the road. It will serve as an anchor when the winds of distraction rise, holding you steady while lesser attractions pass by. Over the years, such faithfulness becomes a habit, and the habit becomes as strong as any iron chain.

Doubt and fear are the deadly enemies of any purpose, Allen warns, and they must be rooted out of the mind without mercy. A man who gives them a place to live has already half failed before he has begun, since they weaken every effort at its source. The courageous thought, by contrast, is the first step of any journey that ends in success.

Mistakes will certainly be made along the way, but Allen refuses to treat them as final defeats. Each failure, he argues, carries a lesson that can be turned into strength, provided the person keeps his purpose and learns to think more wisely. Those who continue to learn in this manner are already travelling toward success, however slowly they seem to go.

When thought is joined firmly to purpose, he writes, it becomes a creative force, and the person who wields it ceases to be a drifting leaf. He takes his rightful place in the world, calm in his power and able to accomplish real work. Such a man has stopped wishing for strength and has begun to practise it.

The fifth part of the book considers the part that thought plays in achievement, which Allen believes is the root of all that people accomplish. Before any bridge, book or business exists in the world, it has first been built in someone's mind. The outward achievement is merely the shadow of an inward effort that came first.

Allen states the price of achievement bluntly: he who would accomplish little need sacrifice little, and he who would accomplish much must be ready to give up much. There is no way of rising without leaving something behind, whether it be comfort, idleness or the approval of others. Great aims, in other words, demand a great willingness to let go of smaller and easier things.

To rise higher, a person must abandon his laziness, his fears and his selfish desires, for these habits are the weights that keep a man low. Each one has to be replaced, patiently, by a better habit of thought, since an empty mind is quickly refilled by the old tenants. Progress, on this view, is more a matter of exchange than of mere subtraction.

The same law, Allen insists, operates in the world of business, in the pursuit of learning and in the life of the spirit. In each of them, the reward belongs to the person who thinks clearly, aims steadily and does not shrink from effort. There are no separate rules for the different fields, only one principle that happens to wear many costumes.

Good results rarely arrive in a day, and so patience becomes a part of the work rather than a pause from it. Allen says that the person who keeps going calmly, without bitterness or hurry, will be standing in the field when the harvest finally comes. The seed does not grow faster because we dig it up to look at it.

The sixth part of the book is devoted to visions and ideals, and it opens with a famous claim that dreamers are the saviours of the world. Just as the visible world is sustained by the invisible, Allen says, humanity is lifted by the unseen dreams of its idealists. Without these dreamers, the labouring crowd would have nothing worth the trouble toward which to labour.

Allen reminds us that every great builder, thinker and teacher began with a vision that nobody else could yet see. Roads, cities and whole bodies of knowledge were once nothing more than a picture held patiently in a single mind. Those who laughed at the dreamer have often ended by living in what he built.

The vision that you glorify in the mind and the ideal that you enthrone in the heart are the very things, he says, from which you will build your life. In time, he promises, you will become whatever it is that you most steadily admire and keep before your eyes. It follows that we ought to guard our visions as carefully as a jeweller guards his finest stones.

Allen pictures a young worker who toils in a narrow, dull occupation and yet carries a vision of a larger and better life. That inner picture fills his thoughts, rouses his ambition and draws him, step by step, toward the place where the vision lives. Gradually the outward circumstances rearrange themselves until they match the dream that came before them.

Every dream, however, will sooner or later be put to the test, and there will be seasons when it seems impossibly far away. Allen counsels us to cling to it with patience, for a dream that survives such seasons comes out stronger and more fully formed. Doubt is the weather of the journey rather than a sign that the road was wrong.

The closing part of the book is about serenity, a deep and quiet peace of mind that Allen calls one of the beautiful jewels of wisdom. It is not the fruit of a single good decision but the result of long effort and honest self-knowledge. Few possessions, he implies, are so well worth having, and few are so rarely found among restless and hurried people.

A calm person has spent many years learning to govern his own thoughts, and the effort shows in the steadiness of his manner. Because he understands how his own mind works, he understands other people better too, and he meets their anger and haste with patient good sense. His presence, in a noisy and anxious world, is like cool shade on a long and burning afternoon.

The restless mind is like a stormy sea that tosses everything about and gives no rest to those who sail upon it. The calm mind, by contrast, resembles a great rock that the waves may beat upon for ages without moving it by an inch. Allen urges us to ask honestly which of the two we are building, day by day, in our own minds.

Near the end, Allen gathers the lesson into three short sayings: that self-control is strength, that right thought is mastery, and that calmness is power. Each of these claims builds upon the one before it, so that the quiet person becomes at last the capable one. They are easy to remember, and, as Allen would say, far harder to practise.

When our thoughts grow wild and restless, he suggests, we should speak to them gently and firmly, as one might to a frightened animal. We tell them to be quiet and still, and then we wait, because calm is not seized by force but invited by patience. Over many weeks, and with a great deal of repetition, the restless mind learns to obey its gentler master.

The message of the whole book can be gathered into a single sentence: each of us is the maker of his own character. The mind is the gardener, thoughts are the seeds, and the life that we are living is the garden in which they have come up. Nobody else can plant it, and nobody else can be blamed for the weeds.

Choose your thoughts with care, for in time they become your actions, your habits and your destiny. Allen's little book is now well over a century old, yet its counsel remains as simple and as demanding as it was when he first set it down. The work it describes is available to anyone, and it can begin this very hour.
